column2: An Italian open pie that has the entire world fiercely debating the acceptability of pineapple in polite society.
Italian noodles that somehow earned a noble name and cult culinary status instead of being a humble side dish for bangers.
A French pastry consisting of 90% butter and 10% air, which shatters into a million flakes if you merely look at it sideways.
A multi-storey culinary tower of pasta sheets, mince, and béchamel sauce that is physically impossible to slice neatly.
A Georgian bread boat holding more cheese and butter than dough, where the only acceptable cutlery is the torn-off crust.
The primary currency of student freezers and a lifesaving frozen staple for bachelors across Eastern Europe.
Georgian soup-filled dumplings; eating one without spilling a single drop of broth is roughly equivalent to passing a citizenship exam.
A long French loaf meant to be carried under one's arm through Paris while romantically dusting passers-by with crumbs.
Slavic cousins of pelmeni that hide either mashed potato or sour cherries inside, turning dinner into a game of roulette.
A crispy deep-fried pastry envelope stuffed with meat and molten broth that fires straight at your white shirt on the first bite.
A round fried meat pie with a little window on top, legendary in railway station buffets and feared by delicate stomachs.
Italian dumplings with lofty haute-cuisine ambitions that might even be hiding spinach and ricotta inside.
Folded Mexican street food that requires tilting your head at a 90-degree angle so the filling doesn't escape onto your jeans.
A heavyweight Mexican tortilla parcel capable of replacing a three-course Sunday roast and a house brick simultaneously.
A cheesy Mexican folded flatbread proving that literally any wrap becomes a hundred times better when toasted with melted cheese.
A ruby-red beetroot and cabbage soup over whose true homeland more blood has been spilled on food forums than in medieval wars.
A fiery Thai soup that brings tears to your eyes from the chillies yet compels you to keep eating while fishing out inedible twigs.
A giant Vietnamese soup simmered for days and served in bowls the size of a washing-up basin, packed with noodles and beef.
A Japanese noodle and egg soup that rose from cheap student fuel to a hipster cult with three-hour queues.
A Japanese fermented soybean soup that looks rather like murky dishwater yet works absolute magic on the taste buds.
A cold Spanish soup that looks as though someone simply forgot to heat up the tomato sauce for the pasta.
A humble Marseille fisherman's stew that eventually acquired posh seafood and the price tag of a flagship smartphone.
A Japanese delicacy that convinced the world to eat raw fish on rice while testing their dexterity with wooden sticks.
A Western take on sushi where the rice is turned inside out, wrapped in cucumber, and generously smothered in mayo or cream cheese.
A ritualistic Caucasian skewered meat dish cooked over embers, whose preparation strictly forbids both vinegar marinades and interference.
An upper-class slab of beef whose price tag depends entirely on how pink you like it and the bull's aristocratic pedigree.
An Austrian meat pancake beaten to the thickness of a broadsheet newspaper and occupying the entire plate.
A classic Slavic pan-fried meat patty that pairs brilliantly with mash and serves as the ultimate benchmark of a grandmother's cooking.
A Central Asian rice masterpiece with meat and spices, where letting the grains turn into mush is a personal insult to the chef.
Italian rice stirred so tirelessly and lovingly that it turns wonderfully creamy while remaining stubbornly undercooked.
A Spanish pan-fried feast of rice, saffron, and whatever happened to be scurrying by land or sea near Valencia.
An Indian spicy yellow frenzy capable of turning any innocent meat or veg into a glorious culinary house fire.
A thick Hungarian meat stew walking the fine line between a very hearty soup and a rather runny main course.
A French vegetable stew that achieved global fame thanks to a culinary-minded rat in a Pixar film.
A Middle Eastern chickpea paste that vegans will happily spread on toast, crudités, other vegan dishes, and life in general.
Deep-fried chickpea balls that successfully impersonate meatballs, much to the delight of vegetarians everywhere.
Middle Eastern spiced mince on a skewer, the noble ancestor of the planet's premier post-pub midnight snack.
A Middle Eastern wrap of pure joy that unites professors, students, and clubbers outside takeaways at three in the morning.
An Italian mascarpone and coffee-soaked biscuit dessert whose name translates as 'pick me up', hinting at a massive calorie bomb.
A cream-cheese gateau on a biscuit base that people order in cafés when they simply can't be bothered to choose a dessert.
A delicate French almond meringue that costs as much as a plane wing due to its notoriously temperamental baking process.
A French choux pastry tube filled with cream that is impossible to eat in polite company without dabbing your nose.
An American chocolate bake deliberately left underdone so it stays fudgy, gooey, and dangerously calorific.
An Italian sweetened cream jelly that ought to wobble seductively on the plate at the slightest nudge of a spoon.
A chocolate cake with a hidden surprise: slice it open and out flows a river of molten chocolate lava.
The plump little round sisters of the éclair, which can be stuffed with either sweet cream or pâté to keep dinner guests guessing.
A flaky, buttery French marvel that guarantees a pound of crumbs down your front after the very first bite.
An Austrian apple and cinnamon roll whose pastry is stretched to the transparency of a prenuptial agreement.
A classic honey layer cake with sour cream frosting that only reaches peak perfection after a day or two in the fridge.
A flaky pastry edifice that acts like an impregnable fortress under a fork, shattering dramatically in every direction.
A snow-white meringue cake topped with berries, named after a ballerina and every bit as light and fragile as her tutu.
An edible modelling clay of almond meal and sugar used by confectioners to sculpt fruits, figurines, and tooth-aching sweetness.
Thick American flapjacks that always appear in a photogenic stack on Instagram, drenched in maple syrup.
Quark fritters whose foolproof recipe is endlessly hunted on social media by cooks battling to stop them spreading across the pan.
Slavic golden suns of batter, the very first of which traditionally goes straight into the bin as a lumpy sacrificial offering.
Grid-patterned treats whose little pockets exist solely to trap the maximum possible amount of syrup or toppings.
An American ring-shaped fried cake coated in bright icing, the chief morale booster for fictional police officers.
Deep-fried Spanish choux pastry sticks traditionally dunked into thick hot chocolate right at breakfast time.
A fiery Mexican pepper capable of running a free demo version of hell inside your mouth to test your character.
A root tasting faintly of soap and cologne, pickled bright pink to cleanse the palate between bites of sushi.
Japanese green horseradish, a pea-sized dab of which instantly clears the sinuses and brings forth tears of regret.
A royal spice that turns ordinary coffee into an Arabian tale, while accidentally biting a whole pod in a stew spells disaster.
The world's priciest spice, hand-picked from crocuses, costing more than gold and dyeing rice a brilliant yellow.
Fragrant tree bark whose aroma instantly conjures cosy winter evenings, Christmas markets, and an urge to buy sticky buns.
A perfumer orchid whose real pods cost a small fortune, while its synthetic twin scents practically every supermarket cupcake.
The herb of discord, dividing humanity into two warring camps: those who adore it and those who think it tastes of soap and crushed bugs.
An aromatic herb without which Italians strictly forbid making Caprese, tomato sauce, or even setting foot in the kitchen.
A piney culinary twig pretending to be a miniature Christmas tree, yet brilliantly complementing roast lamb or potatoes.
The undisputed king of New Year's Eve tables across the former USSR, made by the bucketload and doubling as a pillow for tired guests.
A dish in which croutons and Parmesan cleverly disguise the fact that you're eating plain leaves in a creamy dressing.
An Italian tricolour flag salad of tomatoes, mozzarella, and basil that takes three minutes to assemble yet costs like a masterpiece.
A crunchy vegetable medley where the Greeks couldn't be bothered to dice the feta, simply plonking a giant slab on top.
A layered culinary experiment where salted fish is tucked beneath warm duvets of boiled root veg and mayonnaise.
A Swiss social pastime where guests dunk bread cubes into a cauldron of molten cheese while cheerfully scalding their tongues.
Mexican tortilla chips that serve strictly as edible shovels for scooping up guacamole or melted cheese.
A Mexican avocado dip that turns pitch black at the speed of sound if you forget a squeeze of lime.
A green Genoese sauce of basil, pine nuts, and cheese capable of turning even corrugated cardboard into fine Italian dining.
The ultimate rescue sauce for terrible cooks, capable of rendering virtually any culinary disaster vaguely edible.
The universal tomato condiment without which children refuse to eat pasta and adults refuse to touch their chips.
Either a gherkin-studded sauce made for fish and chips, or raw minced steak with an egg—depending on which page of the menu you're on.
A classic French white sauce of flour, butter, and milk; the backbone of lasagne and the nightmare of cooks terrified of lumps.
A smoky, sweet glaze that transforms any rack of pork ribs into the quintessential American dream.
A pungent condiment whose English version clears your head in seconds, while the French Dijon kind politely tingles the tongue.
Liquid Italian electricity served in a thimble, engineered for a rapid reboot of the central nervous system.
Coffee crowned with frothy milk; ordering one in Italy after 11 a.m. earns you a deeply disapproving glare from the barista.
A milky beverage in which coffee is present primarily for moral support and a faint beige tint.
Powdered Japanese green tea that smells of mown grass and seaweed yet reigns supreme in trendy cafés.
A warm, spiced winter tipple that makes wandering around freezing Christmas markets actually bearable.
A refreshing Cuban highball of rum, mint, and lime that turns a sweltering afternoon into a pleasant, hazy spin.
A Mexican agave spirit whose drinking ritual involves licking salt, downing a shot, and biting a lime wedge.
A thick blended drink that allows cafés to sell three whizzed bananas and a fistful of spinach for the price of a proper dinner.
A French morning dish of beaten eggs that in a bachelor's frying pan effortlessly degenerates into scrambled eggs.
A breakfast staple that stares intently back at you from the frying pan with bright yellow yolk-eyes.
An egg cooked shell-free in simmering water, requiring the chef to master hypnosis and a gentle whirlpool.
An aristocrat's breakfast where a poached egg lounges atop bacon and a muffin beneath a blanket of hollandaise.
The chief dread of childhood breakfasts, whose oaty form mysteriously becomes the secret to a happy stomach in adulthood.
Stale bread resurrected by a bath in beaten egg and milk followed by a sizzle in butter.
A slice of bread scorched in a fiendish spring-loaded contraption that always pops up at the most startling moment.
Dry fodder for the figure-conscious, composed of rolled oats, nuts, and the optimistic hope of fitting into swimwear by July.
Essentially muesli baked with honey until crunchy, which automatically doubles its price tag in hipster brunch spots.
A hard Italian cheese aged for years that smells faintly of gym socks yet makes any bowl of pasta utterly divine.
Delicate white cheese balls bobbing in brine that melt gloriously on pizza and stretch halfway across the room.
A bold English cheese with proper character, the undisputed star of ploughman's lunches, burgers, and mac and cheese.
Mould-ripened cheese whose blue-green veins terrify beginners and delight gourmets alongside a glass of port.
A runny French cheese in a white furry coat that smells of a damp cellar yet bakes into pure gastronomic bliss.
A salty Greek brined cheese born to be chunkily cubed into a salad alongside plump olives.
A creamy Italian whey cheese that impersonates cottage cheese while possessing vastly superior table manners.
A brined Georgian cheese with a knack for peeling into strings and throwing a party inside every khachapuri.
A chameleon soybean curd with zero flavour of its own that obediently absorbs the taste of whatever it's cooked with.
An ultra-rich Italian cream cheese resembling thick double cream; the soul of tiramisu and the bane of every diet.
An American beef patty wedged between two buns that is impossible to eat gracefully without wearing sauce on your chin.
A frankfurter tucked into a soft roll with a tangle of sauces, proving street food can be sheer genius in its simplicity.
Bite-sized chicken coated in golden breadcrumbs, for which children would gladly sell their souls to fast-food chains.
The undisputed king of fast-food sides, whose golden batons mysteriously vanish from the paper bag on the walk home.
Two slices of bread enclosing a filling, named after a card-playing British Earl too lazy to leave the gaming table for dinner.
A continental arrangement of bread and butter possessing the magical property of always landing butter-side down.
A trendy hybrid in which a French pastry is ruthlessly sliced open and stuffed with smoked salmon and avocado.
Exploded maize kernels without a giant bucket of which a trip to the cinema is officially invalid.
Wafer-thin crunchy potato slices consisting of salt, oil, flavourings, and a packet filled with 70% air.
A deep-fried pub snack allowing you to delude yourself that you're eating vegetables when it's mostly batter and oil.
The planet's premier edible antidepressant, neatly divided into 'dark and healthy' or 'milk and actually delicious'.
Burnt sugar and water that, upon meeting a pinch of sea salt, suddenly became the defining flavour trend of the century.
Chewy fruit jellies whose German bear-shaped variety could survive a nuclear winter and remain just as rubbery.
A fluffy Eastern European apple-purée confection that pretends to be a light diet sweet until you check the sugar content.
A crisp French kiss of whipped egg whites that crunches delicately and dissolves instantly into icing sugar.
Hardened sugar on a stick whose primary mission is to keep a child's mouth occupied for thirty blissful minutes of peace.
A posh round chocolate sweet dusted in cocoa powder, named after a subterranean fungus due to its lumpy appearance.
Nuts encased in rock-hard caramel, secretly invented by the Dental Association to stress-test your fillings.
A Middle Eastern sweet of crushed seeds or nuts that crumbles at a glance and demands a full pot of tea to wash it down.
A chewy nut-studded confection that cements your jaws together, ensuring a few quiet minutes during afternoon tea.
A bright red tomato sauce that kids cheerfully squirt over pasta, driving Italian chefs to the brink of madness.
A tart Georgian plum sauce proving that tomatoes don't hold a monopoly on pairing well with grilled meat.
An Azerbaijani reduced pomegranate glaze that elevates any piece of grilled fish into a work of art.
A dark, salty Asian liquid in which overzealous diners drown their sushi rolls until the rice completely disintegrates.
A sweet Japanese glaze that leaves any piece of chicken glossy, sticky, and ridiculously moreish.
A vinegary, fiery American pepper sauce in a tiny bottle, two drops of which turn fried eggs into a Mexican carnival.
A garlicky Asian chilli sauce in a green-capped squeezy bottle that has achieved cult status among spice fiends.
An English liquid mystery with an unpronounceable name and fermented anchovies inside, vital for a proper Caesar salad.
An American-style sponge cake that differs from a humble fairy cake mainly by costing twice as much in high-street cafés.
A miniature sponge topped with a towering swirl of buttercream that cannot be eaten without frosting your nose.
A Caucasian 'Snickers' made of walnuts threaded onto a string and dipped in thickened grape juice.
A flaky Middle Eastern pastry madness so drenched in honey and packed with nuts it makes your teeth ache just looking at it.
Icing-sugar-dusted jelly cubes for which Edmund famously betrayed his entire family in 'The Chronicles of Narnia'.
A thick hazelnut-cocoa paste meant to be spread sparingly on toast, yet universally eaten by the spoonful straight from the jar.
A wobbling, brightly coloured gelatine concoction that looks hilarious until you actually try to catch it with a fork.
Whipped culinary air flavoured with chocolate or berries that vanishes on the tongue before you quite register the taste.
A British culinary wildcard that could mean a silky custard dessert or a steamed suet classic—entirely luck of the draw.
A temperamental French bake that puffs up in the oven with pride and collapses instantly if someone slams the kitchen door.
A velvety sweet sauce of milk, eggs, and sugar that brings trifles and éclairs to life while giving chefs whisking blisters.
A French dessert whose primary thrill lies in shattering the brittle caramelised sugar crust with the back of a teaspoon.
Either a fizzy British sweet powder, a frozen fruit sorbet, or a Middle Eastern fudge—a classic case of culinary identity theft.
A baked treat that successfully masquerades as a wholesome breakfast while packing more sugar than a chocolate bar.
A tall Easter sweet bread studded with raisins, whose white icing and sprinkles are always nibbled off first.
A twisted German baked knot sprinkled with coarse rock salt, the lifelong best mate of a frothy stein of lager.
A coconut-filled chocolate bar convincing you that you're lounging on a tropical beach even on a rainy Tuesday in Manchester.
The ultimate hunger-busting bar of peanuts, caramel, and nougat that famously reminds us we're not ourselves when hungry.
Two caramel-coated biscuit fingers whose adverts forced the world to pick sides between the Left and Right factory.
A nougat and caramel chocolate bar named either after a planet or its creator, though it undeniably conquered Earth.
A fluffy malt-nougat bar that supposedly floats in milk, though hardly anyone has ever bothered to test the theory.
A hollow chocolate egg bought by children and grown-up collectors alike purely for the tiny plastic toy hidden inside.
A spherical lollipop on a white stick whose iconic daisy logo was famously designed by Salvador Dalí himself.
A tangy fermented milk drink cultured with special grains, serving as the ultimate morning-after rescue remedy.
A cultured dairy snack with fruit bits that television adverts suggest is eaten exclusively by smiling women on diets.
Slightly alcoholic fermented mare's milk from the steppes, guaranteed to surprise uninitiated tourists with its sharp kick.
The richest, silkiest top layer of milk, destined to be poured over puddings, stirred into sauces, or whipped for scones.
A lumpy curdled dairy staple that personal trainers insist you eat before bed for slow-release casein protein.
Milk that took matters into its own hands and fermented naturally, becoming the secret weapon for fluffy pancakes.
Soybean curd proving that an ingredient can be completely tasteless yet wildly popular among plant-based diners.
A oozy French wheel that smells of old socks yet transforms into the food of the gods when baked with honey and rosemary.
A regal sheep's milk blue cheese aged in French caves, whose mould holds official haute-cuisine credentials.
Bouncy Italian cheese spheres born to melt bubblingly atop pizzas and stretch all the way to your chin.
A hard Italian classic aged so long it becomes tough as granite and eye-wateringly expensive.
A snowy white Greek cheese without which a Greek salad is reduced to a rather uninspiring plate of chopped cucumber and tomato.
An indulgent Italian cheese that is essentially ultra-thick double cream masquerading as a spread for tiramisu.
A sharp English classic, ranging from pale straw to bright orange, indispensable for a proper cheese toastie or burger.
A light, airy Italian whey cheese as delicate as a misty morning in Milan.
A dependable Dutch cheese classic lurking in every second fridge for emergency mid-afternoon toasties.
That quintessential Swiss cheese riddled with cartoon-sized holes straight out of a Tom and Jerry chase.
A soft French cheese in a white bloomy rind, Camembert's milder cousin and the centrepiece of every posh buffet.
A pungent Italian blue cheese stirred into pasta sauces to drive the neighbours wild with its aroma.
A layered coffee cocktail where espresso is delicately poured into steamed milk to preserve three pristine stripes in the glass.
Coffee engineered for those who find a cappuccino too frothy and an espresso far too brutal.
Espresso ruthlessly diluted with hot water at the behest of American GIs who couldn't quite handle Italian strength.
Coffee paired with a scoop of ice cream—the ideal diplomatic compromise between needing a caffeine hit and wanting pudding.
A heavyweight winter mug so thick a spoon nearly stands upright in it, designed for maximum calorific comfort.
An ancient Chinese leaf infusion that the British brilliantly decided to take with milk, while others ruin it with three sugars and lemon.
A ruby-red herbal infusion from dried petals that tastes pleasantly tart and keeps blood-pressure debaters busy.
An Argentine herbal brew sipped through a metal straw called a bombilla from a hollowed gourd while pretending to be a local.
A zesty citrus refresher that demands a mountain of lemons at home yet comes out of a factory as fizzy sugar water.
A traditional Slavic fizzy brew made from fermented rye bread, refreshing on a scorching summer afternoon.
The world's most famous dark fizzy drink, whose secret formula is guarded more fiercely than state intelligence.
Canned liquid chemistry that promises to give you wings yet mostly delivers palpitations and an all-nighter before exams.
An ancient frothy brew of malt and hops, the chief sponsor of football matches and lively evenings down at the pub.
A noble fermented grape tipple whose price climbs with age and whose bouquet is solemnly swirled by pretentious sommeliers.
French sparkling wine whose cork traditionally aims straight for the chandelier or an unsuspecting guest's eye on New Year's Eve.
A crystal-clear, virtually tasteless spirit possessing the remarkable ability to make everyone in the room sound fascinating.
A Scottish or Irish grain spirit savoured neat or with a drop of water by connoisseurs, and drowned in cola by everyone else.
A pirate's sugarcane spirit and the fiery backbone of tropical Caribbean cocktails.
A French grape brandy meant to be warmed gently in a snifter while swirling it around and pretending to be a philosopher.
An English botanical spirit smelling of piney juniper, virtually undrinkable without a splash of tonic and a slice of lime.
A bitter green wormwood witch in a bottle that famously inspired hallucinations among bohemian Parisian artists.
